item.title: Election 2026: Four candidates seek three seats on Richardson Bay Sanitary District board
item.description: Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens face challenger John Turnacliff for three Richardson Bay Sanitary District board seats on Nov. 3.
item.content:encoded:
Four Tiburon Peninsula residents are seeking three seats on the Richardson Bay Sanitary District board of directors in the district’s first contested election since 2018.

Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens face challenger John Turnacliff. The three winners will serve four-year terms through November 2030, joining sitting board members Mark Slater and Jeff Slavitz.

Board members receive $125 for every meeting they attend and are eligible for the district’s dental plan.

Election 2026:The Richardson Bay Sanitary District board candidates at a glance

Election 2026:Read complete coverage atthearknewspaper.com/election2026

The Richardson Bay district serves northern Tiburon from Gilmartin Drive to Highway 101 and all of Strawberry from its headquarters at Blackie’s Pasture. It collects wastewater across its service area and pumps it to Mill Valley for treatment through the Sewerage Agency of Southern Marin, a joint-powers agency it belongs to with four other member agencies.

Consolidation was the central question the last time these seats were contested, in 2018, and it is again.

Board members voted unanimously July 21 to reject all seven findings and nine recommendations in a Marin civil grand jury report, “Better Service at Lower Cost — Optimizing Essential Services for the Future of Marin,” that urged the county’s more than 50 special districts, including the Richardson Bay district, to explore consolidation. The report found that fragmented districts duplicate administrative work and leave residents with uneven fees and service levels, thin staffing and weaker long-term resilience.

District officials countered that consolidation had already been studied and that the report failed to account for existing joint operations or the financial risks of merging.

The argument predates this board. A 2011 Marin Local Agency Formation Commission report and a 2018 civil grand jury report both concluded the county had too many sewer agencies, and the Richardson Bay board that year opposed even adding language to its response about exploring consolidation of services on a limited scale. In 2012, at the board’s urging, district ratepayers defeated a ballot proposal to consolidate with other member districts of the Sewerage Agency of Southern Marin.

item.title: Election 2026: Measure Z would extend Paradise Cay dredging tax 10 years
item.description: Paradise Cay voters decide Nov. 3 on Measure Z, a parcel tax that pays to dredge the community's canals and its two entry channels to San Francisco Bay.
item.content:encoded:
Voters in Paradise Cay will decide Nov. 3 whether to continue a special parcel tax that pays to dredge the waterfront community’s canals and its two entry channels to San Francisco Bay.

Measure Z would set the tax at $2,200 per lot a year in County Service Area No. 29 beginning July 1, 2027. The rate would then rise automatically by 3% each year beginning July 1, 2028, and the tax would expire June 30, 2037.

The service area estimates the measure would raise an average of about $272,800 a year for maintenance dredging in Paradise Cay’s principal waterways and the north and south entry channels. It needs approval from two-thirds of the votes cast to pass.

Election 2026:Read complete coverage atthearknewspaper.com/election2026

The Marin Board of Supervisors called the election May 19 on a 4-0 vote, with Supervisor Stephanie Moulton-Peters absent. Measure Z would continue an existing special tax scheduled to expire June 30, 2027.

The tax falls on lots inside Service Area No. 29, the county-run district that takes in the Paradise Cay parcels with canal access rather than the whole neighborhood. Keeping those canals and the entrances to the bay navigable requires periodic removal of the sediment that washes into them. Resident Eric Lyons described them as the community’s riparian, or dock-bearing, homeowners. The county has not published how many of the 130 lots pay, though at $2,200 apiece, the revenue estimate works out to about 124.

Lyons has lived in Paradise Cay for more than 30 years and chairs the district’s six-member advisory board. He said the community faces no immediate dredging emergency because its waterways were last dredged in 2020 and 2024. But residents have to keep collecting money for the next project, which the board is planning for 2028 or 2029, he said.

Paradise Cay typically needs dredging about every four or five years, although the precise schedule depends on how quickly sediment accumulates.

“The fill-in depends on many factors, including winter rains, ferry wakes and winter weather in general,” Lyons said. “We’ve never really needed to dredge more frequently than four years, but keeping the north and south cay entry channels clear and wide enough for navigation is always a challenge.”

Dredging Paradise Cay involves more than removing sediment. Projects also carry costs for engineering, planning, sediment testing and regulatory permits. The work needs approval from the ...

item.content:encoded:
Marin County supervisors want a closer look at whether the Strawberry Design Review Board should be restructured or folded into another body. It is one of six such recommendations in a countywide review of the volunteer boards that advise the county.

The board reviews the design of homes and development projects in Strawberry, and it has gone nearly quiet. Since Jan. 6, 2025, the county’s hearing calendar for the board lists a single meeting, on Aug. 17 for a home project in unincorporated Alto. The calendar lists eight meetings in 2024, one of them canceled.

It also has little in front of it. The county lists planning applications by community, and its Strawberry page showed none under review as of Sept. 11. The largest project in Strawberry does not appear on that page either. North Coast Land Holdings’ redevelopment of the former seminary property — approved by the supervisors June 9 and now under challenge in Marin Superior Court — is listed under the neighboring Alto planning area.

A second Tiburon Peninsula body fared better. County staff recommended the advisory board for County Service Area No. 29, which covers the Paradise Cay canals, stay in place with what the county calls governance improvements.

Members of both boards said after the Aug. 25 Board of Supervisors meeting that the county had not contacted them about the review.

item.title: Mallard Pointe tenants move out, but demolition still awaits city permit
item.description: Tenants at Mallard Pointe in Belvedere had to be out by Sept. 14, but demolition of the 22 apartments is still waiting on a bulkhead permit under city review since February 2025.
item.content:encoded:
The tenants at Mallard Pointe had to be out by Sept. 14, but demolition of their 22 apartments is waiting on a bulkhead permit that has been under city review since February 2025.

Belvedere closed one gap last week, hiring an engineering firm to oversee the work when it does start. The city named Petaluma-based Foth its outside project coordinator Sept. 9, filling a part-time post left open after it cut ties with Phillips Seabrook Associates, the firm it hired in April. It will oversee the demolition and the replacement of the bulkhead, the wall that holds Belvedere Lagoon back from the land. The city says Foth will also be an independent check on the developer’s compliance with city code. Belvedere cited the firm’s work on its Beach Road seawall stabilization project.

Planning and Building Director Rebecca Markwick said Sept. 14 that the city is still working on the Foth contract, so its pay and term remain undisclosed. Phillips Seabrook’s April contract was worth up to $200,000 over two budget years.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel
item.media:description: A moving truck is loaded outside one of the 22 rental homes at Mallard Pointe in Belvedere on Sept. 13. The tenants’ 60-day notices expired Sept. 14, but the city says demolition cannot begin until the bulkhead permit is issued and the remaining permit conditions are met. (Ted McDonnell / For The Ark)

item.title: Richardson Bay agency accepts $5 million in grants for debris, eelgrass work
item.description: The Richardson Bay Regional Agency has accepted nearly $5 million in grants to pull sunken debris off the bay floor and replant eelgrass beds that anchors tore up.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly $5 million in grant money is bound for Richardson Bay to pull decades of sunken debris off the bay floor and replant the eelgrass beds that anchors tore up.

The Richardson Bay Regional Agency board accepted the two awards Sept. 10 at Tiburon Town Hall. It adopted both on its consent calendar in a 3-0 vote with Marin County Supervisor Stephanie Moulton-Peters absent. Neither drew discussion or public comment, and the meeting ran 13 minutes.

The larger award, $3,051,000, comes from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s San Francisco Bay Water Quality Improvement Fund and was signed Aug. 13. The agency had asked for $3.95 million.

Under the award, crews are to remove at least 700 tons of marine debris — anchors, chain, sunken boats, batteries and plastics left by decades of anchoring. They are also to restore six acres of eelgrass, survey the bay floor and publish maps of what is down there. The EPA reimburses the agency as it spends, through May 31, 2029. A $200,000 share goes to Sausalito, which dropped out of the agency in May 2017, to measure results and handle outreach.

The second award, $1.9 million from the San Francisco Bay Restoration Authority, pays for a further six acres inside the bay’s eelgrass protection zone, about two years of monitoring and one or two paid internships for Marin students. The agency asked $3.65 million over three years and scaled the work down on the authority’s guidance.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Tiburon producer aims to make scientists rock stars with ‘Particle Fever’
item.description: Tiburon resident Annie Roney is a lead producer of "Particle Fever," a musical about the CERN scientists who found the Higgs boson. It premieres Feb. 16 in La Jolla.
item.content:encoded:
When Annie Roney screened the 2013 documentary “Particle Fever” as part of her job as CEO of the film-distribution company Roco Films, the story resonated with her.

The 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson confirmed a theory nearly 50 years in the making on how particles obtain their mass. But Roney, a 25-year Tiburon resident, says she was equally struck by the way the documentary focused on the scientists behind the discovery at the European Organization for Nuclear Research, known as CERN.

“It gave physics a human story,” Roney says. “It got audiences who know nothing about physics invested in the outcome of these amazing, extraordinary human beings.”

Roney has spent the past decade turning the story behind “Particle Fever” into a musical of the same name. She’s a lead producer of the show, which is set for its world premiere run at the La Jolla Playhouse from Feb. 16 to March 21, with reduced-price “First Look” performances through Feb. 21.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Tiburon resident Annie Roney (left) and Megan Kingery sit on a staircase at CERN’s headquarters near Geneva, Switzerland, in August. The two are producing ‘Particle Fever,’ a musical based on the 2013 documentary about the Higgs boson discovery that Roney’s company, Roco Films, distributed; it opens Feb. 16 at the La Jolla Playhouse. (via Annie Roney)

item.title: Strawberry playground price now tops $3 million
item.description: The Strawberry Recreation District's new playground and restroom are coming in at just over $3 million, more than $500,000 above the maximum the board set.
item.content:encoded:
The Strawberry Recreation District’s new playground and the restroom beside it are coming in at just over $3 million — more than $500,000 above the $2.5 million maximum the board set for the project.

Board members learned the revised figures at their Sept. 8 meeting. They postponed a decision on the restroom contract until their Oct. 13 meeting and told playground company GameTime to come back with a lower price.

From the start of the discussion, Board Chair Peter Teese made clear he objected to the higher price.

“New bid, much bigger numbers, not good at all,” he said. “Like, I’m a hard no, and I’m not going to speak for anybody else, but we started out a lot lower.”
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Two arrested in string of credit card thefts from vehicles at Blackie’s lot
item.description: Two men were arrested on suspicion of stealing credit and debit cards from vehicles at Blackie's Pasture in Tiburon and using them at Bay Area stores, Tiburon police said.
item.content:encoded:
Two men were arrested on suspicion of stealing credit and debit cards from vehicles at Blackie’s Pasture and using them at Bay Area stores, the Tiburon Police Department said.

Several people reported cards taken from their cars at the Tiburon trailhead on the morning of Sept. 5 while they walked the Old Rail Trail, the department said in a Sept. 8 news release. The cards were used later at businesses in San Francisco and at The Village at Corte Madera shopping center.

Officers identified a gray Ford Explorer using the town’s automated license-plate readers. The Explorer entered Tiburon shortly before the thefts and headed toward Corte Madera afterward, the release said. Investigators also reviewed security footage from stores where the cards were used.

Officers found the Explorer at a Strawberry motel early Sept. 6 and detained two men, ages 64 and 55. They then obtained a warrant to search the men’s room. Inside they found newly purchased merchandise, receipts tied to fraudulent transactions, suspected false identification documents and what the department called burglary tools, the release said.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Crib Notes: Belvedere’s ‘house of dreams’ sells for $16.9 mil
item.description: A waterfront Belvedere villa known as Casa dei Sogni has sold for $16.92 million in a pre-auction deal, ending a yearslong effort to find a buyer.
item.content:encoded:
A waterfront Belvedere villa once marketed with a 51-foot yacht and a private dock has sold for nearly $17 million in a pre-auction deal, ending a yearslong effort to find a buyer.

The sale of 125 Belvedere Ave., known as “Casa dei Sogni,” Italian for “the house of dreams,” closed Aug. 21 at $16.92 million, according to Multiple Listing Service records. That is $2.88 million below its final $19.8 million asking price and about $3.9 million more than the seller paid in 2015.

The home was set for sale through Concierge Auctions, a luxury auction firm, with bidding scheduled Aug. 25-31. The buyer made an offer before bidding began, and the seller took it. The buyer also paid auction fees, while the seller paid the real-estate agents’ commission.

The 5,100-square-foot main house has five bedrooms, five full bathrooms and five half bathrooms and an 800-square-foot guest house sits on the 0.41-acre lot. Features include San Francisco skyline views, terra-cotta roof tiles, arched doors and windows, antique Italian fireplace facades and vintage wood flooring from France. The design echoes Portofino, Italy, Belvedere’s sister city since 2016.

Compass agent Steve Mavromihalis, who represented the seller with his team, said the auction was meant to create urgency around a property he believed the market had undervalued after years on and off the market.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: The waterfront villa at 125 Belvedere Ave. in Belvedere, known as ‘Casa dei Sogni,’ sits on Richardson Bay on the back side of Belvedere Island, reached by a pier and a gangway. The Mediterranean-style home, built in 1978 and remodeled to a design by architect Andrew Skurman in 2008, sold for $16.92 million in a pre-auction deal that closed Aug. 21. (Zach Bruce / Lunghi Studio)

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A former jewelry designer recalls key chain that took off
item.description: Mill Valley's Shayala Diamond stopped at Tiburon's Shoreline Park on a 90-degree day. She spent 20 years designing jewelry, including a key chain that took off.
item.content:encoded:
Mill Valley resident Shayala Diamond needs just three words to explain why she’s visiting Tiburon’s Shoreline Park.

“So friggin’ hot,” says Diamond, 73, as highs hit 90 degrees in town Sept. 9. She stopped in Tiburon after the thermometer in her car read 99 degrees, hoping for a 10-degree break.

Diamond has lived in Mill Valley for the past year after spending a decade in West Marin. But she’s familiar with Tiburon, having spent six weeks on Mar West Street during her career as a jewelry designer, from 1996 to 2016.

Her path to jewelry-making has been anything but linear. A product of the 1960s counterculture and its offshoots, such as the evangelical Jesus movement, Diamond met Gurumayi Chidvilasananda in the early 1980s. Gurumayi is the spiritual head of Siddha Yoga, a meditation path drawn from Hindu philosophy.

The experience, Diamond says, saved her — even if she no longer practices the guru’s teachings.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Mill Valley resident Shayala Diamond cools off from 90-degree heat Sept. 9 at Tiburon’s Shoreline Park. Diamond designed jewelry from 1996 to 2016, and the beaded key chains she made in the late 1990s were a hit. She says her business had 40 sales representatives at its peak. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: 65 artists explore lines, textures and marks at Belvedere-Tiburon Library
item.description: The Belvedere-Tiburon Library's new exhibit, "Mark Making: Dots, Lines, Textures," runs Sept. 17 to Nov. 11 with work by 65 Bay Area artists chosen by a jury.
item.content:encoded:
Pat Moseuk is a painter who rarely uses a paintbrush.

To create her contemporary, abstract works, she typically puts paint on canvas with a credit card and makes marks using a wide variety of objects, such as jar lids and hinges.

She says her works are inspired by the grids, geometric lines and shapes found in everyday life and are filled with layers of color.

Residents can see her work on display as part of the Belvedere-Tiburon Library’s newest exhibit, “Mark Making: Dots, Lines, Textures.” The show, which features 65 artists chosen by a jury from an open call to Bay Area artists, runs Sept. 17-Nov. 11. An artists’ reception is set for 6-8 p.m. opening night.

The theme “speaks to reading the layers and texture of a canvas — to trying to discern how the artist’s hand, holding a loaded brush or fingers wrapped around a color pencil, left the marks they did,” says Diane Green, who chairs the library gallery and the exhibit. “Was it intentional or unconscious? This exhibition is, in part, about trying to unpack an artwork.”
item.dc:creator: Diane Smith
item.media:description: ‘Mark Making: Dots, Lines, Textures’ at the Belvedere-Tiburon Library includes, clockwise from top left, ‘Stop Making Sense’ by Pat Moseuk, ‘Wave Chaos at North Beach’ by Sue Dedina, ‘The Republic Proclaimed’ by Advay Mengle and ‘The Astronomer’ by Eduardo del Rio.

item.title: Stephen C. Lynch
item.description: Stephen C. Lynch
item.content:encoded:
Steve was born in San Francisco, the sixth of 10 children born to Raymond and Lois Lynch of Tiburon. Growing up on the less populated side of the peninsula, Steve very early on developed a love of the outdoors and a passion for adventure that remained with him all his life. Fishing at Paradise Park, Sunday ballgames watching the Tiburon Pelicans followed by family swims at the Tiburon Peninsula Club and exploring every inch of the Tiburon Peninsula — the shenanigans and hijinks of Steve, his siblings and friends, remain legendary to this day.

After a short stint at College of Marin, Steve entered the electrical apprenticeship at the IBEW Local 551. With brothers Ray, Gregg, John, Brian and sister Eileen, they continued to build the Edward W. Scott Electric Co. into a thriving Bay Area-wide electrical contracting firm that was started by their great uncle, Edward Scott, and their dad and uncle, Ray and Leonard.

Steve’s fierce pride and joy were his children — Molly, Ryan and Corey. Steve coached many Little League teams and supported the TPC swim teams. He devoted 25 years of very active participation to the Tiburon Volunteer Fire Department, rising to the lieutenant’s position, the highest rank for a volunteer, responding with brothers Ray, Brian and Ed whenever needed.

Steve absolutely loved to fish, and enjoyed many, many years of camaraderie with his fellow anglers of the TAA, Tournament Anglers Association. Annual fishing trips to Mexico, Costa Rica, Hawaii and British Columbia provided such enjoyment! Donner Lake was another favorite spot to fish; those early mornings out on the water feeding his soul.

Steve is survived by his wife, Joan; Molly, Cameron and Kaia Williams; Ryan and fiancée Parin Gallagher; Corey and Casey; and by his siblings Diane, Ray, Chris, Eileen, Gregg, John and Ed. He is predeceased by his sister Kathy and brother Brian. Steve was also dearly beloved brother-in-law to Jim Long, Larry LaFresnaye (d), Kim, Cheryl, Vicki and Alison Lynch, Shana Rohde-Lynch, Tom and Terry Slevin, Nancy and Skip Latno, Cindy and Dan Gallagher and Aileen and Eric Wormood. “Favorite Uncle Steve” is also survived by 24 nieces and nephews, and by Steve’s lifelong, loyal and truly beloved friend, Sam Ware.

The Lynch and Slevin families pray for empathy and a healing journey of hope for all those struggling with addiction. Celebration of Life to be held later this year.

item.title: Tiburon approves $909,000 rebuild of Bel Aire play area
item.description: Tiburon's Town Council voted 4-0 Sept. 2 to spend up to $908,899 rebuilding the Bel Aire play area. It is the first substantial upgrade under the town's parks master plan.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon will spend more than $900,000 to rebuild the Bel Aire play area with an accessible walking loop, a picnic area and new benches — work staff says could be finished as soon as November.

The Town Council voted 4-0 Sept. 2, with Mayor Jon Welner absent, to approve spending up to $908,899 for the improvements, the first substantial upgrades made under the town’s parks master plan. The approval includes an $812,363 contract with Richmond-based W.R. Forde Associates Inc. for construction, plus an $81,536 contingency and $15,000 for construction management and engineering.

“We have a funded park coming to Tiburon,” Vice Mayor Isaac Nikfar said following the vote, which elicited applause from some attendees.

item.title: Election 2026: Health benefits and social-media posts add tension to Marin Board of Education race
item.description: Two Tiburon residents, incumbent Marilyn Nemzer and challenger Avery Lieberman, are running Nov. 3 for the Marin County Board of Education seat covering the Tiburon Peninsula.
item.content:encoded:
Two Tiburon residents are competing for a Marin County Board of Education seat on Nov. 3 in a race pitting the challenger’s attack on the incumbent’s health benefits against his own record of social-media posts denounced as bigoted.

Challenger Avery Lieberman has pledged not to accept the county-paid health insurance if elected, saying the money should go to schools instead. Incumbent Marilyn Nemzer says the benefits are county policy rather than the board’s and that the option lets people of lesser means serve.

Lieberman’s Facebook posts in April described Muslims as invaders and tied them to violence in Europe. He says he was not referring to all Muslims and that he speaks out as a Jewish man alarmed by rising antisemitism. His Facebook posts have drawn accusations of bigotry before: Posts he made about race in 2020 prompted a student complaint at the dental school where he taught. He was notified of his layoff that day and sued the university, alleging it had branded him a racist. The case settled in 2024.

Election 2026:The Marin Board of Education Area 5 candidates at a glance

Election 2026:Read complete coverage atthearknewspaper.com/election2026

The election is also tied to board member Nancy McCarthy, who encouraged Lieberman to run and who has clashed repeatedly with her colleagues on the board.

The contested Trustee Area 5 seat covers all of Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry as well as Corte Madera and Larkspur; the Reed Union School District lies entirely within its boundaries. The winner will serve a four-year term until November 2030. It is the first contested race for the seat in at least 13 years: Nemzer was the only candidate to file in 2013, and no challenger emerged in 2018 or 2022, when she was reappointed by default.

The Marin County Board of Education provides citizen oversight of educational programs and services run by the Marin County Office of Education. It works with the voter-elected county superintendent of schools to set county-office priorities.

Its duties include adopting or rejecting, but not modifying, the elected superintendent’s proposed budget; setting the superintendent’s salary; hearing appeals of student expulsions or denied interdistrict transfer requests; and maintaining positive relationships with the county’s 17 school districts.

The Ark interviewed both candidates in August about their priorities and what they want the board to address.

item.title: Tiburon pastor, radio host and surrogate father Jerry Buckner served generations
item.description: The Rev. Jerry Buckner, senior pastor at Tiburon Christian Fellowship and a radio host, died Aug. 20 at MarinHealth Medical Center in Greenbrae. He was 74
item.content:encoded:
The Rev. Jerry Buckner, a Tiburon pastor, author and radio host who became a father figure to generations of young men, died Aug. 20 at MarinHealth Medical Center in Greenbrae. He was 74.

The cause was neuroendocrine carcinoma, his son Benjamin Buckner said.

Buckner mentored dozens of young men, Benjamin said in an interview, and many of them lived in the family’s home.

Dante Sumpter was one of them. He was 13 in 1989, growing up in Vallejo in a family that battled drug addiction, and he said in an interview that he was lost.

“I was a good kid, but at the end of the day, the choices were becoming this or that,” he said. “A lot of my peers were really disturbed kids that were going through things like me, but they actually were acting these things out.”

Sumpter signed up for a counseling program Buckner ran at Franklin Middle School. Buckner, the senior pastor at Tiburon Christian Fellowship, invited him to church. Then he started making the drive himself.

“He drove all the way from Tiburon to pick me up in Vallejo, Sunday after Sunday,” Sumpter said.

Buckner became a father to him, Sumpter said.

“He introduced me to God in a way that was extraordinary,” he said. “And it made me the man that I am today. Although I am not without fault, I know God in a way that a lot of people don’t know because of him.”

Sumpter, who now works in the optical department at Kaiser Permanente in Santa Rosa and is married with five daughters, is not the only one with stories about Buckner’s influence on his life.

Patrick Peters was 24 when he met Buckner, five years after his mother died. He had grown up in Houston without a father, he said in an interview. He moved into the Buckners’ house and stayed three years.

“(Buckner) was the father that I wish I’d had in my life,” Peters said. “He taught me the true value of family.”

Buckner had lived in Tiburon since 1978. He and his wife, Nancy, were high school sweethearts who married on June 11, 1971, his 19th birthday. They raised two sons and three daughters at The Hilarita apartments. The Ark described him in 2011 as a spiritual leader there. Nancy was a nurse at Marin General Hospital, now MarinHealth Medical Center.

For more than 30 years, his voice went out across the Bay Area on Saturday nights. “Contending for the Faith,” his live call-in program on KFAX AM 1100, took questions about Christianity from anyone who dialed in, and listen...

item.title: Adaptive-signal pilot at Trestle Glen won’t come until spring
item.description: Tiburon's adaptive-signal pilot at Tiburon Boulevard and Trestle Glen Boulevard will not be running until spring 2027, Public Works Engineering Manager David Eshoo says.
item.content:encoded:
An adaptive-signal pilot intended to ease the Tiburon Boulevard bottleneck at Trestle Glen Boulevard won’t be running until spring 2027, Public Works Engineering Manager David Eshoo said. He said that is the pace the town expects, given Caltrans’ review process.

Eshoo gave that update to The Ark after a Sept. 2 presentation to the Town Council on the pilot, which is budgeted at $105,000 to $180,000 in the town’s fiscal year 2026-2027 capital-improvement program.

No equipment goes in until the study is done. Parametrix must analyze how the intersection operates, then settle with Caltrans on what the state will allow and bring a recommended design back to the council. The council would then decide whether to send the project out to bid.

That work started Aug. 12, Eshoo said, and Parametrix began gathering video and traffic data for its analysis of existing conditions the week of Aug. 24. The consultant produced the town’s two-year traffic study and is now coordinating the signal work.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Traffic officials add sixth bus to relieve crowded school routes
item.description: A sixth school bus started running Reed Union School District routes Sept. 8, after crowding left 24 students on a waiting list and 10 of 16 routes over capacity.
item.content:encoded:
A sixth school bus was scheduled to start running Reed Union School District routes Sept. 8 to relieve crowding that has left 24 students on a waiting list and 10 of 16 routes over capacity.

The Tiburon Peninsula Traffic Alliance board approved the bus and a driver at a special meeting Sept. 1, at an estimated cost of $140,000, and amended its fiscal 2026-2027 budget to pay for it. Bus provider First Student was expected to have a bus and a standby driver in place, according to a staff memo to the board, with a permanent driver to be hired later.

The alliance is a joint-powers agency of the town of Tiburon, the city of Belvedere and the Reed Union School District. The vote was 5-0, with board members Liz Webb and Isaac Nikfar absent and Tiburon Town Manager Greg Chanis voting as the town’s alternate representative.

The alliance had budgeted for 850 passes this school year. By Aug. 31 it had sold more than 1,000, leaving 10 of the district’s 16 routes with more pass holders than seats and 24 students on waiting lists across six routes.

item.title: Angel Island burn of up to 260 acres is underway; smoke visible this week
item.description: Smoke off Angel Island this week is a prescribed burn, not a wildfire. California State Parks asks Tiburon and Belvedere residents who see it not to call 911.
item.content:encoded:
Smoke is visible off Angel Island this week, and residents who see it are being asked not to call 911.

California State Parks, Cal Fire and the Marin County Fire Department began the prescribed burn of up to 260 acres at Angel Island State Park on Sept. 8. Ignitions are to continue through the week as conditions permit.

Smoke is expected across the peninsula from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on burn days and for up to three days after ignitions.

The burn targets potential wildfire fuel loads in island grasslands and coastal scrub and is paid for through Proposition 4, the climate bond voters approved in 2024. State Parks also lists invasive-plant management and wildlife habitat improvement among its goals.

Burn days are cleared through the Bay Area Air District, and the operation is called off and rescheduled if wind, humidity or fuel moisture won’t carry the smoke away from surrounding communities. While the burn was underway, the district issued a Spare the Air alert for today, Sept. 9 — for ozone rather than smoke — forecasting the worst air inland, in its Eastern Zone and the Santa Clara Valley.

State Parks burned vegetation piles on the island in late January under the same program and said at the time it might conduct more burns in February.

The park remains open, but portions of the Ida Trail, the Sunset Trail and the park’s fire and perimeter roads close during the burn and for as long as three days afterward. Crews will also bar the summit of Mount Livermore on some burn days.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel
item.media:description: Smoke from a prescribed burn rises off Angel Island at about 1:30 p.m. Sept. 8. Crews are burning up to 260 acres at the state park through the week to reduce wildfire fuel. (Claire McAuliffe)
